subtopic: STATEMENT ON AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED STATES

speakeroldname: Hon. W. E. Harris (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: STATEMENT ON AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in my budget speech on March 14 I referred to the tariff on potatoes, and to procedures which the government had initiated under the general agreement on tariffs and trade looking toward an upward adjustment in the present bound rate of duty.
In this connection we have been carrying on negotiations with the United States. I am happy to inform the house that these negotiations have been successfully completed, and that we are now in a position to implement the results. Later, when the Customs Tariff bill is before the house, I shall be moving an amendment as I indicated yesterday I might. This amendment relates to the potato item and I think I should give a brief explanation of the action being taken.
Since 1939 there has been no Canadian duty on table stock potatoes imported from the United States except for a seasonal tariff of 37J cents per hundredweight from June 15 to July 31. These rates were established by the Canada-United States trade agreement of 1938, and they were bound under the general agreement on tariffs and trade. During the same period there has been no Canadian duty on seed potatoes, but imports of seed have been negligible. The effect of the proposed amendment will be to apply, as of midnight tonight, a year-round duty of 37\ cents per hundredweight on all seed and table stock potatoes imported into Canada, except that new potatoes imported during the period from January 1 to June 14 each year will continue to be free.
In reaching a decision on this matter the government took account of the expert testimony and the conclusions available to it through the tariff board hearing on potatoes, and we attempted to weigh the over-all interests of Canadian producers and consumers.
In regard to our producers, we had to take into consideration not only their views expressed to the tariff board but also the fact that in our negotiations with the United States we were informed that, in so far as we found it necessary to increase our tariff applying to United States potatoes, they would consider it necessary to increase their tariff applying to Canadian potatoes. Our growers still attach importance to the maintenance of export outlets in the United States for a substantial volume of Canadian potatoes.
In regard to new potatoes, the tariff board pointed out that these are imported into this country during the spring and early summer months. The board concluded that they "command a premium because they are new; and probably would enter whether or not they faced a customs duty at the border". In such circumstances a tariff on new potatoes would not be of great benefit to Canadian potato producers, and would operate chiefly as a tax on consumers. There was a further point we had in mind during our discussions with the United States; producers in Florida, California and other southern areas attach a high value to their Canadian market for new potatoes.
The trade agreements to which I have referred provided for certain concessions to Canada on potatoes by way of reductions from the United States statutory tariff rate of 75 cents per hundredweight. Under GATT the United States has been obligated to admit at least 3J million bushels at a reduced rate of 37J cents per hundredweight; this has been made up of 1 million bushels of table stock and 2 % million bushels of seed.
Under the new agreement, and as a condition of getting freedom of action to make the tariff changes which I am proposing, the United States is reducing the present tariff quotas by 1 million bushels; 400,000 bushels will be taken off the table stock quota and 600,000 bushels will come off the seed quota. For the current crop year it appears unlikely that we will be able to take full advantage of either the seed or table stock quota.
It was against a background of reduced exports and increased imports, and following urgent representations from Canadian producers and an inquiry by the tariff board, that the government came to the conclusion that the potato situation was a special one which justified special action. Accordingly we took the exceptional course of renegotiating a tariff commitment under the special procedures provided for in article XXVIII of the general

Potatoes-Tariff Changes agreement on tariffs and trade. We took this course so that it would be possible to implement the results of the renegotiation during the current potato marketing season.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on April 2 I directed a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs concerning the position of the Palestinian police force, and in particular whether it was still under Egyptian control. He said he would require time to obtain an answer. Then on April 3 he asked for further time. Is the Acting Secretary of State for External Affairs in a position to give an answer today?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Acting Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON POSITION OF PALESTINIAN POLICE FORCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before he left the city the Secretary of State for External Affairs mentioned to me that he had promised to give my hon. friend a reply today.
I can say in answer that the Palestinian police force of Gaza is, according to the Israeli-Egyptian armistice arrangements, normally under Egyptian control. Detailed discussions are proceeding, however, at the present time with a view to developing arrangements as to the requirements of the United Nations emergency force for adequate power to stop infiltration and incursions across the demarcation line. The general officer commanding the United Nations emergency force is satisfied with the progress of these discussions.
Information has also been received that the United Nations emergency force will now have full operational responsibility for preventive action at the demarcation line, and that it is not now the intention to employ joint or mixed patrols for this purpose at the line.

speechtext:
I should like to direct a question to the Minister of National Health and Welfare, of which I have given notice. It is based upon an article in the Calgary Albertan reporting a serious shortage of Salk anti-polio vaccine in the Calgary area.
In view of the shortage of Salk vaccine in southern Alberta for use by private practitioners, caused by curtailment of exports of vaccine by the United States, will the government now make available a portion of the Canadian-produced vaccine currently earmarked for public health in order that the medical profession may resume service with this vaccine to Canadians not covered by the public health program?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Marlin (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: SALK VACCINE-REPORTED SHORTAGE IN CALGARY AREA
speechtext:
My hon. friend was kind enough to give me notice of his intention to ask this question. In reply I would say that the current supply and anticipated production of the Salk vaccine in Canada at the Connaught laboratories,
[Mr. St. Laurent (Quebec East) .1
which at the present time is the sole Canadian source, is such as to allow a broadening of the use of the vaccine on a country-wide basis.
On March 22 the Canadian Pharmaceutical Association, the Canadian Medical Association and the deputy ministers of health of all the provinces were notified that under the arrangements we had made with the director of the Connaught laboratories the vaccine would be supplied on request through normal channels to medical practitioners. This will be done without any modification in the delivery schedules by the Connaught laboratories to provincial health departments, in accordance with their respective requirements. All orders thus far received have been filled, and up to April 2 some 50,000 doses of the vaccine have been sent out to all parts of Canada. There is no reason, therefore, why any practising physician should be denied vaccine for his patients.
The distributors for the Connaught laboratories are located in Winnipeg and Vancouver, and vaccine may be procured by retail pharmacists in the usual manner or on direct order by doctors and pharmacists to the Connaught laboratories. In the case of the province of Alberta I have learned this morning that three deliveries of vaccine have been made in Edmonton and one in Calgary.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration. Has the minister had sufficient time to think

it over since his reported meeting with Mr. Foon Sien, national president of the Chinese benevolent association? If so, is he in a position to announce any change in the present policy of excluding the adopted sons of Canadians of Chinese origin?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Pickersgill (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
maintopic: EXCLUSION OF ADOPTED SONS OF CANADIANS OF CHINESE ORIGIN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since there is probably a good deal of interest all over the country in any change that might be made in the policy with respect to the admission of Chinese immigrants to Canada, I might say that when Mr. Foon Sien and the Minister of National Defence called on me the other day I did say that, not as a change in the regulations but as an experiment, since the previous experiment seems to have been working very well, we would be prepared to recommend the admission of the female fiancees of Chinese and also of Japanese residents of Canada after they have been here two years, so they no longer will have to wait until they become citizens.
About the other points that were raised, including the one mentioned by the hon. gentleman, I said that consideration would be given to some of them but that, at the present time, in view of the rather large volume of immigration and the difficulties in dealing with existing applications, I doubted the wisdom of enlarging the categories of persons who would have to be dealt with by the Hong Kong office, when it would simply mean making longer queues. In view of the great burden of immigration in other parts of the world where we are actively recruiting immigrants it would be quite impossible to increase the staff at Hong Kong at the present time with competent people, and there is no use sending people who are not trained to a difficult post like that.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO DANGER OF RADIATION FROM TELEVISION SETS, ETC.
speechtext:
I wish to direct a question to the Minister of National Health and Welfare, of which I have given him notice. First, will the minister inform the house whether or not the research division of his department has found any possibility of dangerous radiation in (a) television sets and (b) X-ray or fluoroscope machines used in some retail shoe stores in Canada? Second, if there is any indication of such radiation, what steps have been taken by the minister's department to protect the Canadian public?
Inquiries of the Ministry Hon. Paul Marlin (Minister of National Health and Welfare): My hon. friend did give me notice the day before yesterday. In answer to the first part of his question I may say that representative types of Canadian television sets have been investigated to determine if radiation from them presents a health hazard. No radiation could be detected emerging from the sets that were studied. My technical officers in the environmental health division are confident that the sets being used in Canadian homes present no health hazard from radiation. This confirms the statement of the British medical research council in their report of June, 1956, when they observed that nuclear and allied radiations did not in this context constitute either a personal or significant genetic hazard to man. In the course of the continuing studies being made by our department of the effects of radiation, my hon. friend may be sure that this matter is under continuous surveillance.
With regard to the second question may I say this. At the end of last session I referred to the report of the technical committee of the United Nations on radiation with special regard to fluoroscopes. In consequence I pointed out that it was desirable that the use of fluoroscopes should be made only in accordance with careful standard medical procedures. It is not within the authority of the federal government to eliminate these fluoroscopes. That is a matter which under our constitution comes under the authority of the provinces. They have been advised of this situation, and I think we may assume that they are taking necessary steps if the situation in Ottawa is an indication of what has resulted. I am informed that at the present time, for instance, 14 of the 21 machines examined a year ago in Ottawa have been discontinued. I would assume that the provinces are taking vigilant action in other communities.

Some irrigation farmers or ranchers who have no grain of their own to sell to the wheat board find a straight grain farmer who is short of dollars and buy a readily saleable grade of wheat at a price considerably less than the legal initial payment price at the elevator, and deliver the grain on their own producer's permit.
In some cases this type of transaction is facilitated by the elevator agent who may do it as a service to his customer or take a cut from both producer and the seller in the transaction.
I believe, sir, the rather serious charge involved here is a matter that would certainly come under the jurisdiction of the Canadian wheat board.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it
is quite legal for one farmer to sell grain to another farmer in the same province; but it is quite illegal for the second farmer to deliver that grain to the wheat board. The country elevator agents are also agents of the wheat board, and I would assume they would be vigilant in stopping that second transaction.
As I say, the policing of grain within a province, when there is a violation of the act, passes to the province in relation to oats and barley. As far as wheat is concerned, I am sure the wheat board endeavours to prevent farmers from delivering grain that was not produced within the area to which their quota applies.

May I ask
the minister a question. There is nothing illegal about one farmer in Alberta selling and delivering grain to another farmer in Alberta for the purpose of feeding that grain to the second farmer's cattle, is there?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Robinson (Simcoe East) in the chair.
On clause 1-

Mr. Chairman, this clause starts with the following words:
All that portion of section 5 of the Income Tax Act following paragraph (b) . . .
I just do not understand how that applies, because there is nothing following paragraph (b) as far as I can see.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Well, Mr. Chairman, I am not sure whether my hon. friend has the same edition of the Income Tax Act that I have, but paragraph (b) has a great many items in it-seven, to be exact-and the concluding words of section 5 are:
. . . minus the deductions permitted by paragraphs (i), (1) and (q) of subsections (1) of section 11 and by subsections (5) to (11), inclusive, of section 11 but without any other deductions whatsoever.
Those words are being struck out and the words of the amending bill substituted therefor. The difference is that we now refer to a (qa) of subsection 1 of section 11. This

Mr. Chairman, the minister said he was not certain if the hon. member for Perth had the same edition of the Income Tax Act that he was using. Perhaps that is the reason some income tax offices make assessments which are different from those made by other offices.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I do not think so.

Mr. Chairman, before this clause carries may I ask the Minister of Finance what conclusion, if any, has been reached by himself and the Minister of National Revenue concerning exempting from income tax the living expenses of construction workers who go to jobs away from their home centres. We had a discussion on this point at the resolution stage preceding the bill. If the minister will remember I suggested at that time that he should consider the question with his fellow minister.
Since that discussion took place I have received a copy of the submission made to the federal government by the Canadian Construction Association a few weeks ago. I find that the attitude of the construction industry itself, as distinguished from the union's was not brought to the minister's attention the other day.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. May I remind the hon. member that we are discussing clause 1, and as far as I can see it has nothing to do with the construction industry.

Well, Mr. Chairman, as Your Honour knows the practice on clause 1 of the bill is to have a fairly wide discussion. This same question was discussed on the first paragraph of the income tax resolutions, and I submit that I am in order in raising the question today because it follows directly the discussion which took place the other day. I merely wish to point out to the minister that the construction association had this to say:
The issue of "Bulletin No. 10" by the Department of National Revenue last summer concerning transportation and living allowances for construction workers sent to out of town job sites has also been the subject of widespread concern in the industry and a number of meetings with the ministers and senior officials of the departments of national revenue, finance and labour. The treatment of transportation allowances has been settled satisfactorily but it is recommended that the Income Tax Act be amended so that construction workers who, because, of the peculiar nature of the industry's operations, are often sent temporarily away from the location where they maintain their home, will not have these extra living expenses considered as taxable earnings.

I do not want to take up any more time of the committee on this question, but can the minister give us any further statement with regard to this problem today?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I was aware of the representation; indeed, I think I was present when the brief to which the hon. member referred was presented. This was only one more element in our study of the problem, because quite obviously the construction industry as such wants to have the friendliest relations with the union members they hire. On the other hand they appreciated the fact that their permanent employees are permitted this deduction and I think they understand why that would be so. The presentation indicates that they would like the exemption extended.
I have not been able to discuss the matter with my colleague the Minister of National Revenue since our discussion the other night, but if hon. members attach some importance to it, as I assume they do, perhaps what I intend to say could be put this way. I would not want the details of the present bill to be held up or to discuss this on any unrelated subject, but I will discuss the matter with my colleague before third reading of the bill, and perhaps I could say something at that time.
I would like to ask the Minister of Finance if these expenses were permitted in the 1955 tax returns.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes.
How was the alteration made; was the act changed or were the regulations changed?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No; it was by a bulletin issued under the authority of the Minister of National Revenue to his officers throughout Canada.
Was this done in consultation with the Minister of Finance and with his agreement?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I do not think we acknowledge either yes or no to that question.

Well, it makes it very difficult for an employee in the construction crew of a company when one year he is allowed these deductions, and then when he takes employment with a company on the understanding that these expenses will be allowed he finds at the end of the year, after the work has been completed and his returns sent in, that they are not allowed. What steps were taken to inform the employee of the changes in the regulations? I think the minister will realize that it puts the employee in a very disadvantageous
Income Tax Act
position, and really takes from him taxes for which he was under the impression he was not liable.
Could the minister give any explanation to the house, or say whether any consideration might be given this matter to see that notice would be given to these people so they would not take employment expecting to have certain exemptions, and then find the following year, when they send in their returns, that these exemptions are not allowed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Any income tax law change, either by statute or regulation, naturally comes as a surprise to some people who are affected by it. Sometimes it is a pleasant surprise, sometimes it is not.
Not very often pleasant.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: There is no need or there is no point in sending out notices saying that we intend to change the law six months from now or something of that kind. We do not usually do that, though some of our changes take effect at a future date. I am sure there is no person in the construction industry, however, who is not aware of the present circumstances, because every organized group of workers, in whatever trade it may be, has considered this information bulletin. Their senior body or union or whatever it may be has made representations. Therefore there can be no question at all about anyone taking employment at the present time while under a misapprehension as to what the situation may be if this bulletin remains in effect.

I would like to ask the
minister to consider a case which I have had drawn to my attention. A man in this case was granted several hundred dollars in exemption in 1955. He took employment in 1956 completely unaware that there was going to be any change, and he continued that employment under the impression that this exemption would still be granted to him in 1956. I would like to ask the minister when notification was given by the Minister of National Revenue as to the change in the regulations.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: My recollection is that it was September, 1956, but I shall find out and, as I say, I would be glad if we did not take the time of the committee on this point which is not in the bill. I will say something about it on third reading.

I would just like to ask whether the bulletin which was sent out in September, 1956, referring to the earnings in 1956, would apply to all the earnings in 1956?

Income Tax Act
I would not like to answer the question for the minister-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I thought you were going to.

But I have a copy of the bulletin here, and it is not dated in September at all. It is dated July 10, 1956, which was in the middle of the summer and after most of these men would have gone out to work.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That just shows how my memory does not stand up to dates with reference to bulletins issued by another department of the government. I find now that the date should be July 10.
But the taxable year starts January 1, 1956.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is correct.

Well, then, any person so employed would be working under the impression that such expenses would be allowed as deductions for income tax purposes and would take employment on that basis. There was no change in the regulations until July, and this affected him retroactively for at least six months. Is that not so?
Carried.

I would like to ask the minister whether he could say anything about this. Does he say or does he not say that he considers it fair for a person to take employment believing that he is going to have this exemption and then, as the result of some order issued by a department of the government, find that taxes are imposed upon him for the six months prior to his having taken on that job?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Well, it all depends. As I say, I do not want to go on discussing a matter which I am going to have to discuss on another occasion and thereby double the time the house takes on this sort of thing. However, if my friend uses the word "fair", all I can say is that any change is unfair to somebody at some time. I know my hon. friend wants changes, though he does not want one under these particular conditions. However, the change in the tax law must affect somebody at a time when he did not think he was going to be affected.
Now, you may very well say that notice should be given on July 10 saying it will apply to the forthcoming construction season in 1958, if you like; but that is a matter, as I have said, that I will discuss on third reading.
But this is to be retroactive, and it is the retroactive feature that I am discussing.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: My hon. friend does not seem to appreciate the fact that we have a timetable to meet, and I have said that I will discuss this matter. Will he not take my word for it? If he will not take my word I will ask him this question. Would you apply this law to those who are working after July 10 for the first time; would you feel that we should tax those people but not those people who were working before July 10?

No, I would not think it
would be quite fair to tax them from July 10 arid then for notice to be given afterwards. I do think at least a little notice should be given. If his tax had been implemented as of July 10 it would not be too bad, if he could know before that he was going to be taxed; but to tax him on July 10 for work performed six months previously is not fair or just, and I do not think the Minister of Finance has answered me. However, if he is going to give us an opportunity to discuss the matter-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Well, I have already discussed it; that is the trouble.

On clause 1,
Mr. Chairman, I would like to ask a question dealing with the specific clause itself. Would the minister explain once more what we are attempting to accomplish in this clause, because I do not even understand the wording of the explanation.

Well, I have not been asked
for an explanation; I was merely asked where the words were in the act, and I did not attempt to explain the amendment. The amendment is quite a simple one if you have time to follow it through.

to feel sorry for myself if we get more complicated.

speechtext: Well, I suppose that is a matter for my hon. friend, although I do not think his law practice extends very much to alimony, as I recall it.
That is right.
Does the minister's?

This means that we are
providing for the husband, and I use him as an example, who has an income which is an earned income and an investment income. On clause 2 would the minister tell me this. Is the separated spouse entitled not only to claim a married person's exemption but to deduct the payment of alimony as well?

On clause 3-Service pension or allowance.

On clause 3, Mr. Chairman, I note that according to the explanation this means that allowances under the War Veterans Allowance Act will no longer have to be included in computing income. Does this really mean anything at all, since with the present ceiling a single veteran is not allowed to have an income of more than $1,000 and a married veteran's total income must not exceed $1,620.
I would ask the minister whether this clause has been inserted in contemplation of raising the ceiling, as has been requested on a good many occasions, for both single and married veterans under the War Veterans Allowance Act. If it is not, then there is really no object that I can see in putting this in the act at the present time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I will point out an object which the hon. member has not thought of. This is for the purpose of saying that a person drawing war veterans allowance payments shall not have to compute them in his income. Thus if he is dependent on another person his 82715-199
Income Tax Act
income will not be brought above a certain amount-it is $950 at the present time- thereby rendering him a non-dependent.
This would also help a war veteran's widow, would it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am not sure. The main purpose is the one I have given; that if the person drawing an allowance is dependent on another person, and if by reason of the allowance his income went above the permissible limit and he would cease to be a dependent, we are saying that in computing his income his payment under the War Veterans Allowance Act shall not be considered. In effect we are establishing a higher ceiling.
I wonder if the minister will give us an example. Would it be a child he would be considering?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It could be a child, or it could be any person claimed for by a taxpayer. But a situation would arise where A would claim for B as a dependent. If B were in receipt of war veterans allowance, and if by adding that to other income, if any, his total income exceeded $950, he would cease to be a dependent. We say we are not going to use the war veterans allowance in computing B's total income. So it would be $950 for all purposes other than war veterans allowance.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Might it apply in the case of someone having a parent or relative in his home?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Oh, yes, there would be cases where one would find, shall I say, middle-aged children who have parents who are drawing war veterans allowance and who are dependent on them in the sense that they live with them and have no other means of support.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Clause agreed to.
On clause 4-Capital element of annuities.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: At the same time that clause 1 was amended the minister sent me a further amendment to clause 4, that line 22 on page 2 of the bill be amended by striking out the word "separation". Is that amendment carried?
Carried.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

On clause 4 as amended, Mr. Chairman, I am not trying to give a short course on this particular act because I do not intend to extend my practice along these lines, but I have had representations from constituents in connection with this matter. With respect to a separated wife who receives alimony payments the husband, if remarried, can claim a married

Income Tax Act
man's reduction or exemption. He can also claim in respect of payments made to the first wife. In the wife's hands, is that classified as income; and second, if so, is she entitled to a married exemption as far as her tax is concerned?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: First of all, it is income and taxable income in her hands, any payment of alimony. Second, if she has a self-contained establishment and supports a dependent she can claim the exemption.

Mr. Chairman, how does this work in with the $1,500 which is being allowed to be applied on annuities? Does this section affect that in any way, whereby the capital and interest on this new $1,500 allowance introduced this year would both be taxable when received?
I do not know whether I have made myself clear. I am wondering this. The minister will recall that this year he announced that there would be $1,500 allowed from income to be put into annuities or pension plans- lay-away plans, as it were-and that the capital should not be taxed as of now, but that later on it would be.
If a person applies that to an existing annuity, supposing he has a government annuity, would there have to be a new contract, and would this section affect that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, perhaps we could leave that until we reach the clause which deals with the retirement allowance, on page 9. In the meantime, as I understand the question, someone has a government annuity on which he has been paying. In the past that payment has been subject, when it was withdrawn, to tax only on the interest portion. Commencing with the change in the law the payment on that annuity becomes deductible for income tax purposes, and I think my hon. friend wants to know whether the whole proceeds of the annuity ultimately received become subject to income tax for that reason. I think the answer is no, with some qualifications. When we come to this other clause we will discuss that.
This clause does not pertain to that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Only in an indirect way. It has to do with something else.

Apparently subclause 6 of clause 4 has to do with exempting the cost of installing services such as electricity and so on. I do not quite understand the words "to the extent that the amount so paid was not paid (a) to acquire property of the taxpayer." Does that mean if it is a capital purchase? Is that what it is meant to mean?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: This is to exclude the application of the benefit of the section where property actually changed title. If it did change title, then it is an ordinary capital purchase and would be subject to the normal laws in that regard. This is to cover the case where a company or a person has to pay to get something, though he does not get anything in return but a service for which he pays rental of some kind in the future.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Clause agreed to.
Clauses 5 and 6 agreed to.
On clause 7-Charitable donations.

Having regard to the amendment proposed to section 27 of the Income Tax Act, I think most members of the house will agree that this is a step in the right direction; but I am forced to the conclusion that it does not go nearly far enough in resolving an increasing problem in Canada. I refer to the providing of capital, whether it be private capital or moneys from governments, to take care of the rapidly expanding requirements for educational facilities, bursaries, scholarships and aids to education for young Canadians. It does not go nearly far enough to make available a sufficient flow of private money from individual Canadians or corporations for the adequate support of organizations like the Red Cross, the Boy Scouts and a host of charitable organizations which are contributing to the building of a better nation.
The amendment suggested here perhaps will stimulate to some extent in the current or in future years the provision of private money through donations to various Canadian charities by allowing any excess of donations this year to be added to the deductions in the coming year. But where donations of corporations may have exceeded 5 per cent in one year or those of individuals may have exceeded 10 per cent, I am sure it would have the effect in the coming year of reducing the donations which the company or individual might be willing to make in that future year so they might take advantage of the excess they are now allowed to write off in the following year.
I suggest that there be an additional amendment to section 27 and that section 27, subsection 1, paragraph (a), subparagraph (i), now reading "in the case of a corporation, 5 per cent of its income for the year" should be amended by striking out "5 per cent" and replacing it with "7J per cent", and that section 27, subsection 1, paragraph (a), subparagraph (i), now reading "in the

case of an individual, 10 per cent of his income for the year" should be amended by striking out "10 per cent" and replacing it with "15 per cent."
While comparisons perhaps are not too wise at times, especially comparisons with the laws of another country, under United States income tax laws a corporation may make donations for charitable purposes up to 10 per cent of its income and an individual may make donations up to 20 per cent of his income. It may well be that these percentages are too large for Canadians to accept at this time. Certainly in the case of most corporations or individuals these percentages go beyond the portion of their incomes they would be willing or able to contribute to charitable organizations.
For some years Canada has maintained its limits on donations at 5 per cent for corporations and 10 per cent for individuals. I feel, sir, that we have now reached a state in our country where the demands for funds are so great that Canada would be well advised at least to split the difference between our present levels of allowable donations and the levels now prevailing in the case of our neighbour to the south. I suggest that we can achieve that splitting of the difference by revising the maximum which any corporation may give to recognized charitable organizations in any year to 7-| per cent, and in the case of individuals to 15 per cent.
Before I go any further, would the minister indicate whether this matter has been considered by the government and, if so, what are the government's views on the amendments I now propose.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I should not like to leave the impression that by suggesting this amendment I am trying to get something by way of tax concession for any individual or any corporation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I did not suggest that.

I think the minister is quite aware, as are other members of this house, that donations to any charitable organization cost the taxpayer money and involve to some extent a loss in revenue to the government.
However, my point is this. As indicated by such recent federal actions as the setting up of the Canada Council, our grants to universities and the increase in various welfare payments, the government of Canada recognizes the fact that there is a need which must be met either by private capital or by government capital, the capital of all the

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
No, I am not prepared to do that, for the reasons I have given. There are perfectly acceptable reasons why corporations or individuals should feel that they might contribute to charitable organizations which will do a great deal of good work and in particular, as my hon. friend has mentioned, for scholarships and the kind of investment that returns money in the long run. On the other hand, these corporations and individuals are, I think, obliged to contribute to the cost of government, the cost of maintaining essential services here, including our cost of defence and indeed our cost of charitable donations in the sense of the exemptions that we now grant in particular cases. It may well be that these persons or corporations would feel that they were doing more for the people of Canada by these donations than they would be doing by paying the money in to the revenues of the federal government. However, that would be a matter of opinion.
All I can say is that the amount of tax reduction we gave this year, as of recent date on tea and coffee, was about the amount of $10 million we have spoken of here this morning. If there were $10 million more to be used by way of tax reductions one would wonder whether it ought to come in a further reduction of sales tax on an item that is in common use by the public, or whether it would be better to allow the tax reduction for the particular charitable purposes my hon. friend has in mind.
I only say that as at present advised I think we ought not to extend this exemption. Indeed I think we ought to look forward to a time when the government will be spending more on these things itself. There is a great increase in the amount being spent this coming year by the government on projects which have a long-term value, such as the Canada Council and additional sums in the estimates for research and the matter of scholarships also. Whether or not this is going to be another case of finding that when the government invades a field private donors leave it, I do not know. But certainly the need is there, and between us we ought to be able to meet it somehow. Nevertheless I feel that for the moment we cannot go beyond what we have done.

I should like to make one further comment. Under an amendment to the succession duty act which we shall be considering later today the government is going a further step along the way of encouraging Canadians to turn over a portion of their estates to charitable causes in Canada, by giving some relief from succession duties on the amounts which are contributed to charities on the death of the owner of the estate.
By making further concessions by way of reduction in succession duties it seems to me we encourage Canadians to give up part of their estates or all of their estates to charity on their death. Why not go one step further and recognize that it is better to encourage Canadians during their lifetime to give more liberally to charitable organizations and to educational causes in Canada? If we are prepared to give up some federal government revenue derived from succession duties by making concessions in the succession duty act-in other words, if we are willing to give Canadians concessions if they are prepared to give parts of their estates to charities on their death-why should we not encourage them to do the same thing during their lifetime by accepting the recommendation I have just made?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall clause 7 carry?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I wish to say something about subparagraph 2 of clause 7 along the lines of the discussion yesterday. This is the subparagraph that has to do with the allowance for the expense of a full-time attendant for a person who is necessarily confined by reason of illness, injury or affliction to a bed or wheel chair.
As the minister knows, and as all hon. members know, we have discussed this on previous occasions, as the result of a ruling of the Exchequer Court of Canada denying a taxpayer the right to claim deductibility because his wife was confined by reason of illness, injury or affliction for most of the time to a bed, but part of the time to a chair that did not happen to be a wheel chair.
I have given further thought to the matter since the minister spoke on it yesterday, and it does seem to me he should consider changing the word "wheel" to the word "invalid". I draw his attention to the fact that he does not narrow the definition of "bed". He does not say it has to be a particular kind of bed. He does not rule out a person who might be confined to a couch. Anything that is a bed meets the condition of the subclause. Yet when it comes to the chair he insists on a wheel chair.
Income Tax Act
I appreciate the point he made yesterday that one does not want to open up this clause too widely, but surely the point is not the construction of the bed or the chair to which a person is confined; surely the point is that the person is a permanent invalid, is permanently ill, or at least in that condition for a full 12-months period. I plead with the minister once again to consider changing the words "wheel chair" to "invalid chair". We suggested yesterday that it might read just a bed or chair. The minister thinks that goes too far. Surely my suggestion that it should read "invalid chair" or "invalid's chair" is reasonable.
I have considered again the wording of the judgment which was handed down in the case to which reference has been made, and it is clear that the judge himself was surprised that the wording was there. He admitted he had to stick to the strict letter of the law in making his decision. It does seem to me that the judge was inviting parliament to be sensible on this point and change this wording from "wheel chair" to something that would take care of the kind of case which was recently considered by the Exchequer Court of Canada.
Has the minister given further consideration to this matter since yesterday, and is he now prepared to respond to the suggestion of the judge that parliament should be sensible on this point?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Chairman, I have given consideration to it and I am not prepared to make a recommendation because, as I understand the evidence in this particular case, while the comments the judge made with respect to "wheel chair" were made no doubt for the purpose of drawing attention to what might appear to be an oddity in the law, the evidence before the judge was that the lady was outside the house. That might well have been the reason she should not get the benefit of this particular deduction; that she went for drives, and that while he was commenting on her sitting in a rocking chair, he was drawing attention to that phase of the case. Whether or not he rested the judgment on that alone and ignored the other evidence I do not know, but I am told that the woman in the particular case was not confined to her bed or to the chair; she was outside the house during the time.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, surely the minister is now going beyond the problem that confronts parliament. I quite agree that if a person claims deduction and does not meet the conditions of that deduction, the department in the first instance and the income tax appeal board and the Exchequer

Income Tax Act
Court of Canada can govern themselves accordingly. Surely we have an obligation to make sure that the definition in the act is a sensible one.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I agree with that, and I can quite understand that someone might feel that this additional advantage ought to be granted to anyone who is confined to a house by reason of illness. But if you are going to make it go that far-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: And the requirement of a full-time attendant.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
And the requirement of a fulltime attendant-we have never thought that we ought to go that far. When this amendment was introduced not so long ago it was on the plea of a great many hon. members that we ought to consider the extreme cases, not the ordinary illnesses but the extreme cases. And the extremity determined was if you were confined to a wheel chair or to your bed for a period of 12 months.
As I said yesterday, one might make the remark that that is being too extreme; that it ought to be six months, or less than that. I am not prepared at this moment, until I am far better acquainted with the kinds of cases on which claims are made and granted, to extend the advantage, recognizing as I do that it does seem a little strange that we would not put in any type of chair. The wheel chair was put in for a particular purpose. It defined right away a great many people who could take advantage of this as being persons who were confined to wheel chairs.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: May I ask the minister this question. Surely in what he said earlier he was not objecting to persons who are permanent invalids, confined for most of the time to their beds and their homes, being taken for a ride once in a while?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Well, this is just the kind of remark I would expect from my hon. friend when he-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: It is the minister's remark I am commenting on.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
My remark was that one does not object to sick people getting out in an effort to get well, or even to spending some pleasant hours outside, but the purpose of the original advantage was to cover the person who is confined, not one who is out. Now, I am not going to suggest that because a doctor finds that his patient in 11 months has progressed so well that fresh air and a new interest in life would be of advantage should say to this person, "No, you stay in bed for another 24 days and you will qualify for the tax deduction and then I will let you out." But these are the kinds of things you
TMr. Knowles.]
ought to have in mind when you make your laws, and the very reason I have said it does not take on a large but a clearly defined group, before you move on to another one.

Mr. Chairman, I am trying to cut through some of the arguments I have heard on both sides now on this particular question, and it seems to me that the minister and his department are fully protected by the restricting nature of the other provisions in the same subclause. It refers to "full-time care in a nursing home of the taxpayer, his spouse or any such dependent". Then it says, "throughout the whole of a 12-month period". Surely these first two requirements pretty well take away any possibility of persons attempting to take advantage of any small loophole in the rest of this Clause.
I read the case in question, Mr. Chairman. I think the judge very definitely did point out this particular feature, perhaps not as a deciding issue in connection with the case but as a very definite warning that conflict was going to arise in the future over this very thing. As I read the clause now I can see someone who, say, is well enough to be lifted from a bed and placed in a wheel chair, otherwise complying with all the other requirements, and taken out along the street in a wheel chair in the sun, or whatever is necessary or whatever can be done. On reading this section I see the case of a person who has to be lifted from bed and placed in a stationary chair in a room where there may not be a wheel chair, and complying in all other respects with this clause; yet there is no provision to cover that case or if there is a provision it is a discriminatory one.
I think in view of the two other restrictive parts of this clause the words "wheel chair" might well be deleted, or certainly something along the line suggested by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre substituted.

Mr. Chairman, I think this
clause could be rewritten in some manner and still meet the objective of the minister. There are some people who when placed in a wheel chair outside can go all over the garden lot. There are others who have to be lifted into a chair. It may be a morris chair or an arm chair or something of that nature. They cannot move or propel themselves or anything of that nature, but can be lifted into a morris chair, wheel chair or rocking chair for a short time in order to rest out of bed. Perhaps after an hour or two they must be placed back in bed.
I know what the minister is trying to accomplish and I think it is quite right, but I believe if the wording were different he

could accomplish what he is attempting to do and still meet what the hon. member has just spoken about. I just point out that the wheel chair is not a limitation, because those who occupy them can go any place they like. In many cases they can propel themselves and are infinitely better off than a person who has to be lifted out of bed and placed in an arm chair. I think the minister should consider rewriting that clause.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I am very grateful for the
comments of the hon. gentlemen. It seems to me that what really happened here was that the lady got out of the bed. The judge went one step further and said that getting out of bed in itself vitiates the advantage of the tax concessions, but it would not have done so had she got into a wheel chair. If the original premise is correct; namely if parliament intended to allow an exemption to two groups of persons, the first being persons who have been confined to bed for 12 months-and I do mean confined to bed, because that is what the section says-then unless there have been administrative regulations with which I am not familiar this lady would not have lost the advantage by getting out of bed.
There is another group of quite obviously paralysed persons or disabled persons who do not have to stay in bed but can get around with a chair, so we said we would give that group the advantage of this also because primarily they require an attendant, so there is nothing unusual about this judgment. The judge says in effect, "If you had been fortunate enough to be able to get into a wheel chair I might have been able to find in your favour," though I do not know how many of these Sunday afternoon drives or other things would have to take place before the judge would have felt he could not grant the exemption.
Let us leave it this way. I think the hon. member for Lanark has agreed with me that it must be a genuine benefit for a very needy group of people, and that if we are too restrictive, if we should not have these groups just confined to a wheel chair because they are paralysed and need an attendant or are in bed and need an attendant, if there is an in-between course we will try and find what it is.

Mr. Chairman, I intended to ask a question about the first part of this clause. How does the minister define, "housing corporations resident in Canada"? Does that mean that the buildings which the corporation constructs are in Canada or does it mean the corporation must hold a charter from one of the governmental agencies?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I could explain that when we reach clause 14. It is the same group.

Mr. Chairman, I think perhaps the point I want to raise was referred to on a previous occasion. If that is the case I shall have to go through Hansard and look it up. I want to refer to the $100 deduction for charitable donations. It occurs to me there is an unfairness about this in one respect. A person is allowed a deduction of $100 for charitable donations to start with, and he can claim that $100 even though he has not given a dollar. This means that the person who is generous and gives, let us say, $500 is really credited with only $400 compared to the other person who claims $100 and has not given anything. I think this provision is unfair in that respect.
I am not saying that the person who gives $500 should be credited with a donation of $600, but I think it is unfair that the person who is a mean man can claim $100 even though he has not given a nickel. The generous person who gives $500 to his church or to the Red Cross or some other charitable organization is given $100 less credit than the man who does not give a thing. It seems to me there should be some balance of fairness there.
Why should not the man who does give to charitable institutions be allowed $100 the same as the mean man, plus credit for any other amount in excess of that which he might give? Perhaps it would be fairer if it were provided that a person cannot claim $100 without supporting his claim with receipts. That would solve the problem. However, that is not what I understand is going to be the case. I understand that a man can claim $100 even though he has not given a nickel, and he is not required to produce any receipt, while the fellow who does donate generously to charitable institutions does not receive credit for that $100. Does the minister not agree that there is an element of unfairness in this provision?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Chairman. That is one of the considerations we had against doing this. It is quite obvious that a citizen who considers that his contributions to charitable organizations or religious bodies or his union dues ought to be more than $100 will feel that this provision is an advantage to someone who not only does not contribute proportionately as much as he does to these desired objects but does not even contribute the $100, and takes a slight tax advantage to the extent of his tax rate on the difference between his total donations and the $100.
However, when we looked over the tax returns, as I indicated in my budget speech,

Income Tax Act
we found that in the group who would be affected by this we had, X think, 70 per cent of the persons filing tax returns. There would have been some who had no contributions of any kind but there were a great many, I think, who had contributions almost up to the $100, so there was a real advantage from the standpoint of the efficiency of the department and the cost of operating the department, not to speak of the convenience to the public in providing this exemption.
I can only say that we could not think of any step to take to add to the advantage of the citizen who makes generous donations except the one we have passed just now, providing that if he gives above his limit he may carry the balance forward to the following year. I can only say that those of us who are paying the $100 will feel that some persons are having something from the government. As my hon. friend the member for Winnipeg North Centre said yesterday, this is in effect a further exemption of $100 added at the bottom for a group of people and not for the whole of the taxpaying public.
However, on the medical side you may well find a person who perhaps does not pay the full $100 for other purposes but does need it for his medical expenses; and we thought on balance that this would help considerably in the busy months of April to July or something like that, as well as the year round, and that even if we were granting a straight tax exemption to some persons we were at least reducing the tax load. I might add that we also were aware that there would be argument made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and others that this ought to be recognized as a true exemption, and that these donations should be treated as further deductions over and above the $100.
Will the minister tell the house whether any person who has not paid $100 in charitable donations is compelled by this change to collect the $100 if he has only contributed perhaps $50.
There is a high sense of morality there.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am not sure how the form will be made up, but I fancy it will provide for a standard deduction worded in such a manner that there will be no offense to one's conscience for taking advantage of it.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, usually when words are put into one's mouth by someone else a complaint is registered. I register no complaint; I accept the words which the minister has put in my mouth and which indeed are based on what I said yesterday while we were on the income tax resolutions.

I feel that the government should have given consideration to the two requests that have been made in parliament and outside of parliament; namely that the statutory exemptions should be increased and also that something should be done relating to the 3 per cent floor under medical expenses so far as income tax deductibility is concerned.
The minister in our view tried to effect a compromise between these two requests, and in effect he has met neither of them. So far as the change being an increase in the statutory exemption of only $100 is concerned, that hardly meets the increased cost of living or the reduction in the value of the dollar since the present figures of $1,000 and $2,000 were set for single and married taxpayers respectively. I hope still further consideration will be given to the need for a greater increase in the statutory exemptions than $100, and I hope, too, that consideration will still be given to the justification that people have for expecting tax consideration for the three types of expenses or contributions which are mentioned in this section.
As my hon. friend the member for Macleod said, in line with what I said yesterday, there are those who make heavy contributions to approved charities and who will not be given preferential treatment as against those who make no contributions. The same point has to be made regarding trade union dues and also dues to professional organizations. When the amendment was made in 1951 or 1952, I believe it was, to provide for trade union dues to be allowed deductibility, that was a recognition of the part that is played in our national life by those who contribute membership dues to trade unions and to professional organizations. That recognition and that consideration of what these people do by keeping going these voluntary and democratic organizations is now more or less wiped out, because everybody will get $100 covering this kind of thing anyway; and I think this is, in a sense, defeating the recognition which was accorded by the previous decision.
As I said yesterday, we cannot but welcome tax relief of any kind which is given to our people, but it seems to me that this proposal, rather than meeting the proper request for consideration of the medical expense matter and the proper request for some amendment to the trade union dues clause, to cover all trade union dues, is really just a little token toward the demand for an increase in the statutory exemptions. All sorts of bodies and organizations are suggesting that the statutory exemptions should be raised from $1,000 single and $2,000 married to such figures as $1,500

single and $3,000 married. The minister has tried to meet these requests and these demands by an increase to $1,100 and $2,100. This may be typical of my hon. friend, but it is not good enough.
Could the minister inform us how much loss of revenue the department will suffer by the blanket use of the $100 exemption?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Do you mean the standard
deduction of $100?

In other words the department, I assume, has calculated what the difference will be between the situation had they continued on the old course of allowing small individual receipts to be filed with them and deductions permitted, and the amount they will now collect allowing an across the board exemption of the additional amount.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The figure we considered was $32 million as a minimum and $38 million as a maximum.

Income Tax Act
unfortunate mistake in the distribution-the bills got into the Senate boxes, I am told- and in any event there was not time to fathom the real significance. I trust the minister will regard this as a reasonable request.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Well, if as we go through there are some things which the hon. member feels we should allow to stand over I will be quite agreeable, because I recognize the difficulties. While I thought we would be able to get the bill distributed last evening we were not able to do so in some cases. However, I would just like to make a brief explanation about clause 8 and then we could adjourn, and my hon. friend could think it over during the lunch hour.
This is a case of two non-resident corporations, each of which owns a subsidiary in Canada, and the two non-resident corporations are merged, or amalgamated, or what you will, so that one non-resident company then has two subsidiary companies in Canada. Under those conditions the present law does not provide for that tax relief on the designated surplus which it would if they had not merged. All this does is provide that a single company taking the place of two parent companies should have the same advantage as if the merger had not taken place.

I should like to express my gratitude to the minister.

On clause 14-Certain housing corporations.

Could we have a word of explanation about clause 14 and the two new paragraphs? The explanatory note says that they are to provide for the exemption from income tax of the organizations described therein. Perhaps it is self-explanatory. We understand what is involved in the case of the national conference of Canadian universities, but when it comes to low cost housing accommodation are these non-profit organizations?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: This is to provide that there will not be income tax payable on the income of a corporation providing low cost housing accommodation for the aged. speechtext: I am afraid I do not quite understand the relationship of the tax element to the mortgage financing of the construction. Perhaps I have not understood my hon. friend.

Possibly I am working under a misapprehension, but I was given to understand that the minister had received a certain request from a group or from individuals with regard to this matter. request was that the loss incurred on account of the brokerage fees and the discount should not be subject to income tax. I hope I have made myself clear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
I move:
That bill 407, an act to amend the Income Tax Act, be amended by striking out lines 1 to 7 on page 10 thereof and substituting therefor the following:
(ii) an arrangement under which payment is made by an individual
(A)	in trust to a corporation resident in Canada, of any periodic or other amount as a contribution under the trust, or
