contracts providing for the payment to or to the credit of the holder thereof of a fixed or determinable amount at maturity, of any periodic or other amount as a contribution under any such contract between the individual and that investment corporation, to be used, invested or otherwise applied by that corporation resident in Canada or that investment corporation, as the case may be, for the purpose of providing to the individual, commencing at maturity, an annuity for life.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
May I make a brief explanation, Mr. Chairman. This is to bring within the scope of the amendment institutions known as investors' security institutions which in return for a contract under which a periodic sum of money would be paid to them, similar to payments on annuities and the like, would at some future date repay a fixed sum of money either with or without additional benefit by reason of the investment of these funds. We have found this seems to conform to all the requirements in the proposal with respect to retirement allowances, and we felt that we ought to include them in it.
I did not intend to make any general statement on this matter. I covered the intention of the plan in the budgetary speech at greater length than normally one would deal with it on the budget. I did so for the purpose of informing the public and the house as to what we were trying to achieve. The pages which follow page 9 are our first effort at it. I have no doubt whatever that improvements can be made in the drafting and in the plan as we go along. However, we have presented that basic plan on which no doubt there will be refinements in the future. If hon. members have questions, of course, I shall be glad to answer them and to accept for study any suggestions to improve the minimum plan that we have presented here.

There are one or two basic questions I should like to ask. First of all, as I read the section and inform myself as far as I have been able to do so about similar plans elsewhere, it would appear that from a practical point of view this will be primarily carried out through arrangements with insurance companies. That is, as I understand it, the way it has been done in Britain and possibly elsewhere. That leads me to ask one or two questions with that thought particularly in mind. On page 9, as I read down the page I come to the word "premium", the definition of "premium", and I find this language:
(e) "premium'' means any periodic or other amount paid or payable under a retirement savings plan, ...
Would that apply to a single premium insurance policy?
Income Tax Act

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes. That would apply to any payment, even if it is not a periodic payment; so that theoretically a person may buy an annuity with a lump sum payment, but of course that payment would not be wholly deductible. It would be deductible only to the extent I mentioned, namely 10 per cent or $2,500.

As I come down further I come to paragraph (h) on page 9, "retirement savings plan" and I find this:
(h)	"retirement savings plan" means
(i)	a contract between an individual and a person licensed or otherwise authorized under the laws of Canada or a province to carry on in Canada an annuities business, under which, in consideration of payment by the individual of any periodic or other amount as consideration under the contract. that person agrees to pay to the individual, commencing at maturity, an annuity for life, or . . .
I should like to read the next subparagraph:
(ii) an arrangement under which payment is made by an individual in trust to a corporation resident in Canada of any periodic or other amount as a contribution under the trust, to be used, invested or otherwise applied by that corporation as trustee for the purpose of providing to the individual, commencing at maturity, an annuity for life.
Reading those two paragraphs together and adding to them the amendment the minister has moved, may I ask how wide a range of corporations that would involve. For instance, would it include trust companies or banks, or would it include any corporation as well as the kind mentioned by the minister a few moments ago? Would it really include any corporation with which an arrangement is made and which comes within the scope of the act?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
We are going to try to carry out the plan in the broad sense rather than the narrow sense. If any company or trust company can show that they conform with the intentions we have tried to describe, of course their plan will come within the ambit of the act. But it seems to me there are three rather obvious groups. There is the life insurance company; there is the government annuity; and then there is the investors' syndicate that I mentioned a few moments ago, which in fact issues a written agreement which on the face of it is an agreement to refund a certain sum of money at a fixed date, and so on.
I should say there is a fourth group, namely the professional groups which were referred to in the budgetary speech and which, because of the nature of their association, could act as trustees for the members of the association in accepting these payments and investing them for the purposes that we have in mind.

Income Tax Act
These appear to be relatively obvious and simple. But then when we move into the trust companies which today, as I understand it, make a practice of issuing guarantee certificates which are only a guarantee of the repayment of the money at a future date and some specified interest rate in the meantime, we find that these companies would not conform to our requirements. If the trust company then found it possible within its charter or by amendment to it under the provincial legislation and subject to any condition that the provincial government might impose, and chose to sell contracts similar to those which I happen to know are now being sold by the investors' syndicates, for example, I am quite satisfied that we should accept that as conforming to the requirements of the bill. I think it is obvious that some trust companies may feel that this would be a desirable branch of their business and may take steps to do it. But at the moment I am not aware of any that have such a plan in existence, though they are making inquiries and will no doubt consider whether or not it is in their interest to do so.
The minister used the phrase "payment of a sum of money". I imagine he meant by that payment of a sum by way of annuity.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Oh, yes.

Then my next question is this. Suppose any individual trust agreement were entered into, let us say, with a bank or trust company whereby that institution undertook to take money, to invest it and, at the end of a certain time, contracted to pay an annuity. Would that not come within the ambit of the clauses the minister has read?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Yes. The purpose is that at a fixed period of time, at a certain age of the individual, he would then begin to receive an annuity for life. I think we would be fairly careful in authorizing, if I may put it that way, particular plans, having in mind the trustee concerned. I think you will find that anyone who could set up a business that appeared to be responsible to do this would come within our requirements.
As I understand it, the banks are not now in a position to do this. They accept money for deposit and in some cases it is not withdrawable except on certain notice, and in other cases there is a checking account that can be used all the time. But if they were to accept money which could not be withdrawn but which could be used in that manner for investment, and were to make a contract for the payment by way of annuity at a future date, I see no reason why we

could not accept it. That is why I say I do not know of any bank that is capable of doing that at the moment, though there have been inquiries from them as well.
Is the person who accepts the money and enters into the contract necessarily a corporation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Those that we think at the moment can do so are corporations, but it is conceivable that the professions might prefer not to have their own guild, so to speak, act as trustee and might appoint someone for that purpose. If so, there would be no objection to that.

In his speech the minister said, as I understood it, that an annuity of this kind would not be assignable. I draw the minister's attention to line 12 on page 11. I take it that the reason for the annuity being assignable, apparenly, is when it is assignable by will?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes, I think the words are "by will", not "at will".

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Can the minister make a few comments with regard to government annuities in relation to this addition to the Income Tax Act, and say whether this change effects any change in the income tax treatment accorded government annuities at both ends? Perhaps I might be permitted to say we are glad to note that the rate of interest applied to government annuities has at last gone up to 4 per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I thank my hon. friend. As I said the other day, if he stays here longer he will find that we go on doing things in the proper manner.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: And as I said, how long, O Lord, how long?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Oh, yes; but there has to be, along with the genuine desire to do something, the capability of doing it.
To answer the first question, Mr. Chairman, the present annuity will not be interfered with in any way. Payments which may be made on it in the future may be deductible for the purposes of these provisions; but to the extent of that payment, and the claim for deduction that may be made for it, there would be an alteration in the taxation when the annuity is paid. I think that is logical, and I think my hon. friend agrees.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: May I ask if that is optional. Does the taxpayer decide at which time he wants the deduction?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
At the moment he has his contract which provides for income tax on interest when it is paid. He can now opt

to claim deduction subject to the conditions I have mentioned, which will be spelled out in the regulations, or he may buy a new annuity which would come wholly within this and would not have to be divided.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: In other words, if a person who has had a government annuity for some time and has not been claiming, or been entitled to claim, deduction for the payments he has made in, now chooses to do so, he can claim deduction for those payments from now on? I note the minister is agreeing. Does it follow that there will have to be some complicated formula to determine what the rate of tax will be when that person draws his annuity benefits later on?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes. I am not an accountant and I really have not explored this very much, but it would seem to me that when the annuity became payable there would be several ways of doing it. A simple calculation would be to take the total amount paid in by way of premium and pro rate the amounts paid out by the claim for deduction as against those for which there was no claim for deduction. On the other hand, there may be other means, and I have in mind the proportion from year to year that the person claimed by way of deduction of that particular payment. I am not in position to say which is the formula, but it will be a very complicated one.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: May I ask whether that right to choose either way would apply to annuities purchased under the amendment now before the committee?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
As I said in my budget speech, this would apply to any payments made since the beginning of this year, and we have not been able to work out a formula to apply to existing contracts other than government annuities. In fact, as I say, we have not the formula for that either, but we have our thinking completed on it. The insurance companies have been of great assistance in this and in other points on the various kinds of endowment policies, annuities, and the like, which they have issued, and we are consulting with them to find a suitable formula.
Now, the purpose is to encourage savings and to that extent go back beyond this year. If we do not adopt as deductible in the future some payments on existing contracts, it will not be because we do not approve of them as a means of savings but only that we find it difficult to work out a formula that would be fair to those who from now on might buy new contracts and therefore come wholly within the terms of the contract.
Income Tax Act

In clause 2 (a) (i) I find the following:
The plan does not provide for the payment of any benefit before maturity, except by way of a refund of premiums.
If a plan should be devised which provided not only for an annuity payment for a stipulated number of years but for a payment in case of total disability to commence at that time, which might be five years or 10 years before the ordinary annuity payments might begin, would it mean that such a plan could not be worked out because of these provisions, or would that be considered as a maturity date if such a plan were worked out? I think what we are all interested in here is to see a plan by which people ordinarily can do something about looking after themselves. If there is no such plan in existence at the moment I am sure the companies which would be involved in this type of thing will be striving to cover every conceivable circumstance as they go along. I am wondering whether this would prevent the working out of such a disability provision in an annuity contract.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I think I understand my hon. friend to suggest that if there is an annuity contract which provides for the commencement of the annuity payment at, say, 20 years from the date of the contract, and if total disability ensued in the meantime we should permit a deduction not only of the premium but of the accumulated benefits of the plan up to the time of total disability.

No; the minister may have misunderstood my question. What I am asking is this. If such a plan is devised and benefits are started under such a plan not at the end of the 20-year period but at the time total disability arises, would this clause prevent such a plan being approved?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Well, the purpose, of course, is to provide annuities and not to provide some kind of insurance.
I understand that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
And, as I take it now, if a contract has been purchased from an insurance company which provides for a form of savings plus an insurance against disability and the contract matures upon disability, would we permit it within the terms of this provision rather than saying that because the disability occurred earlier than the fixed period that we have in mind, therefore it does not qualify. I must say that this is one of those details the insurance companies are preparing for us, and while I would not

Income Tax Act
want to suggest that we can agree to it, yet, as I said before, there is a great deal of detail to work out.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
There is one other suggestion I should like to make arising out of the minister's assurance, if I understood him correctly, that generally speaking the purchaser of a government annuity will now have the choice as to the tax treatment of which he wishes to take advantage.
My suggestion arises from the fact that I have noticed some of the insurance companies are already advertising contracts under which they purport to pass on to prospective purchasers the benefit of this portion of my hon. friend's budget.
Might I suggest that the minister suggest to his colleague the Minister of Labour that the advertising of government annuities include reference to the fact that in addition to the new 4 per cent figure there is this choice of tax treatment, which it seems to me is an advantage. The income of most people is certainly greater during their working years, during the years when they are making payments into a fund, than it is during the years when they are drawing out. Accordingly, although one does not know what the tax rates will be in future decades, generally speaking it is a greater advantage to be able to claim tax deductibility when one is paying in to a pension or an annuity than when one is drawing out.
I would hope that this improvement, for that is what it is, with respect to government annuities will be given the proper advertising and publicity it deserves. If my hon. friend the Minister of Labour is a little shy about doing that sort of thing he could take some lessons from my hon. friend the Minister of National Health and Welfare.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am sure the Minister of Labour will read my hon. friend's remarks; I will even suggest that he might do so. However, I would not want to recommend to him that he follow the advice given, because I am in the unfortunate position of always urging my colleagues not to spend as much money as they do and I would not want to be inconsistent.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Now, now; the minister
checks a few dollars but spends the millions.

Mr. Chairman, am I correct in understanding that it will be possible for the department to work out a situation where you have an insurance policy which is mixed insurance and annuity. Can the department break that situation down?
I do not want to go into more detail on this but I have noted here some questions as to the effect, let us say, on an endowment policy

of an insured member under the present plan. For instance, what effect will it have on the right to surrender the contract for its cash value? Will that be abrogated?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I think the clause we have just been discussing covers that. We shall accept the plan if-line 11 on page 10-"it does not provide for the payment of any benefit before maturity, except by way of a refund of premiums." The repayment or cash surrender value would have the effect of obtaining a benefit from the policy, or the annuity if you will, before maturity and we do not contemplate that happening here.
It would not be possible to do that and have a readjustment. I presume the same would be true with regard to a loan on the policy?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes.

Mr. Chairman, I move:
That Bill 407, an act to amend the Income Tax Act, be amended

Mr. Chairman, I wonder if the minister has another copy of this amendment. I might suggest that when copies are being made it could perhaps be borne in mind that there is a group of 15 men in this corner of the house who would like to have one, and we frequently miss out on them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am extremely sorry. I thought I provided a copy for each party in the house.
This has happened on other occasions, and I do not blame the Minister of Finance any more than some of the others.

Mr. Chairman, by way of general comment on this clause I might say I do not think any hon. member of the house could disagree with the purpose of this particular amendment to the Income Tax Act. That purpose appears to be the encouraging by every possible means of exploration of the mineral resources of this country, this particular measure of encouragement being extended to those companies now engaged in the processing of mineral ores in Canada.
I gather from the comments of the industry in regard to this amendment that its probable immediate value will be to further encourage such projects as the aerial survey which is now getting under way in the Ungava area of northern Quebec and Labrador, and also to encourage certain of the mining or processing companies who have engaged in exploration work and expect to expand this activity in Ontario, northern Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta, British Columbia, the Northwest Territories and the Yukon.
Inasmuch as this amendment extends to those companies now processing mineral ores in Canada the same right to charge off against their taxable income the actual costs incurred in the exploration for minerals, in addition to other forms of liquid or gaseous minerals such as oil and natural gas, I and my colleagues in this party certainly agree wholeheartedly with the extension to our processing companies of the concession which has been applied to oil refining companies and certain other mineral processing companies over recent years.
However, I would like to say again, as I have in previous years, that I do not think the concessions provided under the Income Tax Act and the regulations pertaining thereto which are designed to encourage the exploration and development of mineral and other resources in Canada by Canadian companies go far enough.
In discussing this clause I cannot deal in detail with the particular so-called concessions, except to say that the recent report of the Gordon commission did go a long way toward endorsing certain of the recommendations which have been made in this house by representatives of my party over the last few years, designed to encourage more Canadian investment in Canada's resource development.
Income Tax Act
This particular development does take one big step forward along that road. I only hope that before the Minister of Finance brings in another budget, if he has the right to bring in another budget in his present capacity a year from now, he or the next minister of finance will adopt more of the suggestions made in this house by members of my party, and will also adopt the recommendations made by the Gordon commission in order to give far greater encouragement to a faster development of Canadian natural resources by Canadian companies and Canadian individuals.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I do not want to talk out my own bill, but I do want to say that we were aware of the fact that the Gordon commission was going to look into this particular problem, and that is why last year I postponed discussion of this particular matter, which has been raised regularly since I have been Minister of Finance.
The taxation and depreciation allowances and things of that nature for persons who are engaged in exploring for our natural resources in order to produce them for the benefit of Canadians, and for that matter for the benefit of the world, apply to an industry in which all Canadians are greatly interested, not only for the profit which it may bring and the improved standard of living which will follow, but because it is proper that our resources be used for mankind. Now, in the case of persons who explore for these natural resources, especially in the western provinces, there exists, according to their views, an inequity. I have been deeply conscious of this and if I can make the same answer to my hon. friend as I did this morning-and I notice he rather carefully did not mention the United States laws in this connection during the last few minutes-
I would be happy to mention certain United States laws if the minister wishes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
All right; but the Gordon commission has made certain recommendations, some of which at first reading perhaps could not be adopted, others of which might be, and we have been paying particular attention to this part of the report. We have been studying it ourselves and using persons who are well-trained in accounting and things of that nature to see if there could be an improvement made in the present law, so that if there is no discrimination against Canadian companies it will be made clear to them why there is no alternative, and if there is, we might find a solution which would make it less difficult for them to conduct their explorations in competition with companies which, in the main, have more money

Income Tax Act
to begin with and through the operation of some of the present laws may appear to have more money left out of these years of operations for future exploration.

Mr. Chairman, I know there may be very few companies in this category, but if we had the situation where a foreign corporation, under our tax laws, was considered as doing business in Canada-and there may be a few in that situation-would it be entitled in computing its tax for these purposes to take advantage of this regulation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: We did not have them in mind in presenting this amendment; we had in mind Canadian companies.
Canadian corporations?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes. I do not know that we had so defined them, but I am under the impression that that is so.

Yes. I think, Mr. Chairman, I would like at this time to subscribe to the views expressed by the hon. member for Calgary South and to say that this is certainly a step in the right direction, especially since we are dealing with a concession perhaps not in connection with the actual fabrication of goods, but certainly the term "processing" is applicable. That is a situation which we have been stressing for some time. It seems to us that the more we can process the natural resources which we dig out of our soil, the very much greater is going to be the benefit to our economy.
I do not like to get into the same class as my hon. friend to the left to whom the minister has already referred in reference to the taking of an extra step at each concession along the road, but I assume there are very many more ways open to us to assist Canadian companies to ensure that the whole processing and fabricating of these natural resources takes place in Canada. I think if we keep this in front of us each year as these budget resolutions come along and legislation follows, it will help everyone.

There was one question I
would like to put to the minister in respect of part of his answer to my previous comments. He said that serious study has been given to the Gordon commission report and recommendations to the government on the tax laws as they affect the national resource development. I mentioned something along this line a year ago in this house, and I recall that in answering my speech at the time, dealing specifically with the so-called tax concessions on natural resources, the minister said that since the Gordon commission was sitting

at that time it might not be advisable to make any change in the regulations or in the act until after the Gordon commission findings had been submitted.
Now that the preliminary report is out, and I presume the detailed follow-up report will be available shortly, can we take it that the government will in the very near future be giving detailed consideration to the Gordon commission recommendations with regard to natural resource development and particularly the tax laws applying thereto? May I also take it that the government may be counted upon in the next parliament to bring forward specific recommendations and further amendments to the Income Tax Act to achieve the things which I am sure the government will agree are highly desirable; a greater rate of natural resource development of all types in Canada for the benefit of our country as well as all the world, and a greater proportion of the development being undertaken by Canadian companies who are given at least as great a measure of encouragement as is now provided to foreign capital under foreign tax laws.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Well, as my hon. friend said in his earlier remarks, there is of course no certainty that I will be Minister of Finance in the fall, but I can assure him that a Liberal minister of finance will consider the Gordon commission report through the summer and fall, and will discuss it in parliament.
Twenty years from now.

There is reference to

Customs Tariff
ground. In the latter case it would mean that those potatoes could not enter Canada duty free.

I believe that the trade made with the United States is a very good one. I think the people of my province are going to be quite happy about it. I am too. Under the schedule there will be only one duty on potatoes coming into Canada from the United States while there will, of course, be two rates of duty on Canadian potatoes going to the United States. If Canadian producers go over the quota-

Yes.

Customs Tariff

I want to say another
word or two because this matter affects my constituency and neighbouring constituencies in the province of New Brunswick. It also affects the province of Prince Edward Island. We had arrived at the point where we were being flooded with United States potatoes, but when the minister and the government really got down to business in my opinion they did a very good job. I hope that the results will be as favourable as the changes would seem to indicate. It looks like a very good move. I may have said some harsh words with respect to this matter in the past but they may have had some weight in bringing the fact before the government that this was really a serious problem to the people of my constituency and New Brunswick generally and had reached a very critical stage this spring. speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: I too wish to join with the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton in expressing the appreciation of the growers of Prince Edward Island to the Minister of Finance and his officials for working out such a satisfactory solution to this vexed problem. It is one which has been annoying the potato growers of Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick for two or three years now and I am indeed happy that it has had this very fine conclusion.

May I be associated with those in our group who have spoken in respect to the recognition that the minister has given to this particular problem. I well recall in 1953 when I first came to this house raising this question and saying that it looked like a rather difficult task at that time. I think the minister has done an excellent job. I am satisfied that the people of the country will recognize it as such. I have not had an opportunity to study the schedule as it is set out, but I expect that it will fairly well meet with the desires that the potato men in the country have expressed. Certainly it should help the industry on the Pacific coast. While I realize that we are bound possibly to lose in the decrease of the amount of potatoes we sell in respect to the seed quantity, nevertheless I feel as I did last year. When I spoke then to this question I think I suggested that if the Americans really want good seed potatoes they are still going to buy them in spite of the additional tariff they will have to pay.

It is rather difficult to follow this schedule. We were handed a typewritten sheet about five minutes ago and it is rather difficult to follow the matter and to know exactly just what has happened. I am wondering about seed potatoes, item 7Id. Can the minister tell us what change is made there in the tariff and also what change was made in the quota in order to achieve this tariff change?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Item 71d was formerly free under the British preferential tariff; free under the most-favoured-nation tariff; and free under the general tariff. The change now is to 37J cents, 37J cents and 75 cents per hundred pounds.
Thank you.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: This is a real gain in the negotiations in return for which, however, we were obliged to agree-as has been indicated-to a reduction in the total quota from 3,500,000 to 2,500,000 bushels. I should say that the horticultural council and those who represented the potato growers agreed with us at the beginning that they could not expect to obtain the benefit of a tariff without some concession being given; and it was agreed that in the long run the best way to do that was in the reduction of the quota. Although I have not spoken to them in recent days I think the figures that we have negotiated were agreeable to them. At any rate they said so when they were here early in December and I have been working on that assumption since then.

May I ask the minister one question? It may be that he cannot give this information but has he any idea how many bushels of new potatoes were imported from the United States? Has he any statistics on the number of new potatoes that were imported into Canada from the United States, such as those coming under item 83b?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The last year for which we have figures is 1954-55; that is for the crop year 1954-55. Total imports were 4,846,243 bushels of which new potatoes represented 1,523,714 bushels.
What about seed potatoes; have you the figures on the importation of seed potatoes?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes. About 100,000 bushels.

I just wanted to say a word on this matter. I listened to the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton who has more interest in this matter than those in my section of New Brunswick. However, we are all interested because it is the big agricultural crop in New Brunswick. I cannot say

that I am as optimistic as is the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton. I am more willing to wait and see just what will happen. As the minister knows and as does everyone else, a very abnormal situation exists at the present time with regard to potatoes. We have the exchange situation which makes the United States sale in Canada more profitable for the United States farmer. Also I believe the price in Canada has been higher than that in the United States, something which does not occur very often. This year is an exceptional year. Compared with the situation we have had before, of course this is an improvement. But the situation was so weighted against Canadian potatoes in the past that almost any change in the tariff at all would be an improvement as far as the Canadian farmer was concerned.
I should like to ask the minister this question. He mentioned the quantity of new potatoes which came in, I think, in 1954 and 1955. I wonder whether he could give us a breakdown of the quantity that came in each month from January until June. Also, what is the situation with regard to what we might term old potatoes-I just forget what term is used here; I think it is "mature potatoes" -after June 14. We have had a tariff against our potatoes in the United States for the whole year except from June 14 until the end of July. Under this new schedule there is a tariff in favour of United States new potatoes from January 1 to June 14; it is against the mature potatoes. After June 14 will mature potatoes from the United States come in at the same rate as that at which they came in previously? According to the statement which was given to us by the minister mature potatoes coming in from the United States I think would be in the proportion of about two to one with respect to new potatoes. I would just ask the minister whether he could clear up that situation and let us know what we could expect.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader

speechtext: The same as it was before; no change.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The exception is for new potatoes during the period January 1 to June 14. My hon. friend has said, "the same as they were before". That is not so. They were not subject to tariff before and they now become subject to tariff.
I was asking if that were true.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
It is true that the tariff has gone up on mature potatoes during that time. I have a very complicated statement
Customs Tariff
on imports of potatoes which I understand is published year by year in one of the trade periodicals. Rather than read the statement I suggest that I could refer my hon. friend to that document and in fact provide him with one in order to show the imports. I think it is fair to say that in the last three or four years there have been evidences, as the tariff board found, that there has been a shift in the potato trade between the United States and Canada. In fact, this is what prompted the potato growers to ask for protection. They had formerly felt that the United States market, particularly the seed market, was so attractive to them that the terms of the agreement which was negotiated in 1938, as I recall it, were to their advantage.
It continued to be so certainly during the period of price support control in the United States after the war and during the period when production had not yet caught up with consumption; but beginning sometime- perhaps if I said 1948, 1949 or perhaps 1950 I would not be too far out-it does appear that production methods in the United States and the demand for potatoes there, with the consequent surplus that occurs from time to time, made the Canadian market more attractive and excited more interest in the United States exporter than formerly was the case, so that in recent years the Canadian producer has had to reassess his market. That was one of the striking features of the representations which were made by the producers, namely that they now feel that the Canadian market was more important to them than the United States market to the extent that at any rate they could not afford to have the Canadian market taken from them to the extent that it had been on occasions. They said quite frankly that they wished to have this protection even though it meant the possibility of their not being able to take advantage of the United States market to the extent that they had heretofore.

The United States exporter can export new potatoes to Canada from January 1 to June 14. Does that period not cover practically all the time that the United States would be producing new potatoes? So far as that is concerned he has not lost anything and Canada has not gained anything; it is practically the same as it was.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: All I can say is that none of the potato representatives suggested that that was so.

The minister has the record of the imports of new potatoes by months. Would it not indicate that on the schedule the minister has before him?

Customs Tariff

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It does indicate, of course, that Canadians have a taste for new potatoes later in the year and during the winter under some conditions; but the real threat to the Canadian market is not the new potato problem at all, it is the accumulation of the mature potatoes which come on the market any time from December until the present time. Perhaps some of this is caused by anticipation of what may happen. The weight on the Canadian market has been most noticeable since February 1 and it resulted from mature potatoes that were harvested in the fall, not the new potato that comes forward during the winter months.

In relation to the last question asked by the hon. member for Royal, am I correct in assuming that item 83 (a) which refers to potatoes in their natural state, covers new potatoes except during the period January 1 to June 14? That is to say, if a United States shipper wanted to send new potatoes into British Columbia after June 14 when our local new potatoes would be coming on the market, the new potatoes from the United States would be subject to a duty of 37J cents? Is that a correct understanding of the matter?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is quite correct. There are just two kinds of potatoes, namely those in 83 (a) and those in 83 (b). The class in 83 (a) is the class which catches all potatoes in their natural state. Item 83 (b) exempts all new potatoes that come in during that period of time. Perhaps by way of elaboration of what I said I should add that Canadian new potatoes rarely come on the market until late in June.
The essential point of 83 (b) would be to make available to the Canadian consumer during the period January to June 14, if they wished, new potatoes that could not be produced on Canadian soil.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is right.

Just one further question, if I may. I wonder whether the minister would give us a few words of explanation as to why potatoes, dried, desiccated or dehydrated, are to be admitted duty-free on a year round basis, as I understand the item at the bottom of the schedule amendments to read. Is there any particular reason for that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The obvious answer I could make is that we were not asked for it, but that probably would not satisfy my hon. friend. All I can say is that it does not seem to have been a problem to the Canadian producer, either the potato producer or the chap who would turn it into a manufactured product such as described in 83 (e).
The point I had in mind was whether generally speaking potatoes were not processed in that manner in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: If they are, they are not having any difficulty with competition.

The amendment reads:
Section 2 shall be deemed to have come into force on the 6th day of April, 1957, and to have applied to all goods mentioned therein imported or taken out of warehouse for consumption on or after that day and to have applied to goods previously imported for which no entry for consumption was made before that day.
That would be tomorrow. Will this apply to potatoes that come in now, or are in the wholesalers' warehouse or are in the retail stores?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
First of all, this is a little
unusual because I think for the first time, in my memory anyway, a change in the custom tariff has been made in the daytime so that something could happen today that otherwise might not happen until tomorrow had the announcement been made at eight o'clock at night. This means if potatoes have come into warehouses in Canada or are here but have not been cleared by customs, they will be subject then to the duty tomorrow or at whatever time they are cleared for customs.
That is what the minister intends, "no entry for consumption" to mean? It means entry for duty purposes?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is right.

One word with respect to
71 (d). I can understand the point which the minister made and the fact that there had to be a certain amount of give and take in arranging any deal such as this. In the constituency from which I came originally we were one of the largest seed potato-producing areas in the Dominion of Canada. That, of course, has altered to some extent during the last few years because of production problems; but nevertheless the certified seed potato industry is still an important one there and we now have the protection. We also have a reduction in the quota. Time alone will tell how this works out. I hope, and apparently the industry hopes, that it will be of substantial assistance to them. I welcome this because I think it is a step in the right direction in providing more protection for the primary producer. If one had time and the circumstances were different one could elaborate on that to a very great extent.
The minister referred to the treaty of 1938 and there were subsequent treaties after that, whereby the protection at one time accorded to the Canadian farmer has been pretty well

whittled away. As the minister knows, the horticultural council made representations this winter, not only with respect to potatoes, which is a specialized field, but with respect to the whole problem of the marketing of fruit and vegetable products and the distress selling which goes on in this country. It is a very easy thing for the United States producer to do selling in the United States behind tariff barriers and get a fairly good price for the great majority of the products, and then to dump the end product on the United States market, which technically is not dumping in our market, and our markets are wrecked by this distress selling of potatoes and other primary products which come in here at the end of the United States season and the very beginning of our own. I think that sooner or later, and I believe soon, the government of Canada will have to reconsider this problem and will have to fix a value for duty purposes of these United States products which are brought in here and which I say technically are not being dumped under the impact of the act, and yet actually are being sold at distress prices.
Of course this is not the same type of duty but because it does represent a beginning of recognition of the problem I am sure it is welcomed by all. We believe and hope it will be of material assistance to the potato industry itself.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
The proposed
amendment to the bill to amend the Excise Tax Act is as follows:
That schedule 3 of this bill be amended by substituting for the words "potted, flowering or bedding plants, dormant flower bulbs and cut foliage" appearing under the heading "Farm and Forest", the following:
"Potted, flowering, or bedding plants; dormant flower bulbs, corms, roots and tubers; cut foliage;"

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance

That is correct. Everything that was spoken of by name the other

night particularly in the bulb line has been added specifically with the exception of the phrase, "cut flowers".

In other words, the ferns that you get in a bouquet of flowers are exempt from the sales tax but the flowers themselves are not. What is the basis for making that distinction? Is there not far more wastage in the flowers than there is in the foliage? After all, this question of wastage is a very serious one. On the west coast there are a great many flowers produced. For example, at the present time there would be a great many daffodils for sale. They are even sent back here to cheer up some of the unfortunate easterners. Why should that exemption not be allowed on these daffodils?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
This subject underwent considerable debate the other night and I do not think I can add very much to the explanation that was made then to the effect that cut flowers were not regarded as an item that prior to other things which continue to bear sales tax should have such a tax taken off.
The cost to revenue is of consequence; I understand it is considerably more than all the other items referred to combined and it was not felt, as I say, that in advance of a tax reduction on some other items which are not in the schedule it should be recommended at this time.
Mr. Pallet!: How much would it involve if that were taken off? It is a very small amount, I understand.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
We estimated that it would be well over $1 million.
Mr. Pallet!: Well, there was an expression made famous in this house a few years ago about that very same figure, and having regard to the benefit that would accrue to the flower growers and the like, I do not think you have given this matter full consideration. Certainly it seems to me to be rank discrimination when you apply a tax for only a part of one type of business and I believe that your cost of levying it is going to exceed the amount of money you collect. I certainly foresee many cases where the growers will refuse to pay the tax and there will be some nice litigation arising out of this use of the word "foliage". The litigation, in my opinion, will cost the government more than the money they say they would not collect and I think it is a very ill-considered recommendation.

may take anything he likes-I cannot account for his misunderstanding of my words.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman as the parliamentary assistant has said, this is the usual type of resolution that has* been received each year since 1952 when the capital structure of the company was changed. As a matter of fact, I am impressed again, as I always have been, by the amount of money required to be spent to carry out
* See correction of figures at page 3198, column 1.

Canadian National Railways the operations of both our national railway and our national air line. I think what we should note, however, is that we have had a profit position with regard to the past year's operations of both the railway and the air line and that we are looking forward to a profit position during the coming year. I think the officers and the employees of the companies should be commended for the efforts they have made in bringing about this happy situation.
That does not mean, of course, that we may not have a few criticisms to offer in connection with the situation as we find it. Personally, I would have liked very much to see the Minister of Transport in the house at the moment because I am thinking of the Questions I asked him about the St. Lawrence seaway a few hours ago during the question period and I recall the very short shrift I got when I requested certain information about the estimates and about a few million dollars that we were expending. I have no intention of taking advantage of the very one-sided opportunity to debate during the question period at which time the dice are all loaded very much in favour of the cabinet, but it seems to me that when we are being asked to vote these large amounts we should at the same time have a fair amount of openness with respect to answers when we request -information from time to time about where ithe money is going and why the estimates may not be quite as they were when the minister came before the house to get his money.
There are a few things with regard to the operations of the railway and the air line which I think might be pointed out. I said last year, and I think it bears repetition, that the railway finds itself almost continually in a rather severe price squeeze. During the committee hearings this year I was very much impressed by Mr. Gordon's statement that the applications for freight rate increases always seemed to be about one step behind the cost spiral with which the railway, in concert with all other types of industry, is faced these days. As found at page 61 of the minutes of proceedings and evidence of the committee on railways and shipping, I asked Mr. Gordon a question about this matter. This was my query:
On the basis of the interim increase you have been allowed, are you running ahead of your increases with your wage contracts, or are you already behind?
Mr. Gordon replied:
I have said in the report somewhere that- where is that paragraph-that the increase in our wage costs was more than in the freight increase we have.
Then he went on to quote the paragraph which is in these words:
[Mr. Hamilton (York West) .1
The additional revenue which these rate increases produced in 1956 fell substantially short of meeting the additional costs of higher wages and other benefits and Increased material prices incurred during the year.
There is an indication here that so far as the requirements of the railway are concerned, there is no opportunity to anticipate with respect to wage costs. As a matter of fact, I think Mr. Gordon's answer was very intelligent. He said that they could not very well anticipate or the costs might be even more than they would be as the result of a straight, open negotiating and bargaining session. The situation might be disclosed and there would be no great benefit to the railway if it were done that way.
Here is one handicap under which the railway is operating. It operates under a system whereby it has a fixed price for its product but the costs in making up the product vary from day to day. At the same time, the railway has an additional handicap. Mr. Gordon has pointed out that it is most difficult for the railway to finance in the same way as ordinary business companies. He has referred to the source of funds and has pointed out that the Canadian Pacific railway has a much greater opportunity to finance additional undertakings by retained earnings. Of course, in the case of the Canadian National the legislation provides that all money arising out of a return on equity must be turned over to the government each year, no matter whether the amount is large or small, and the railway must come back here as the source from which to obtain its funds.
We must also realize that the railway is an amalgamation of a large group of companies which were bankrupt and at the commencement of the operations of the company that fact certainly placed a handicap on the officers and employees in attempting to get the company into a proper position. However, we should note one very encouraging thing. The lines of the company being in a more northerly area than those of the Canadian Pacific it was thought for a great many years that they would be non-productive lines to a great extent, but Mr. Gordon now suggests that the pendulum may be swinging the other way and with the opening up of the northern areas of the country I think everybody is looking forward to the time when the Canadian National may begin to be a most profitable railway operation. In the whole report of the minutes of proceedings and evidence of the committee I think that is the most encouraging statement to be found there.
In that connection there is only one thing I should like to say. With that prospect before us and with the hope that the line will now become really profitable, I hope we will not attempt to saddle the railway with

a lot of extensions and branch lines necessitated by political pressure and political interest. It seems to me that Mr. Gordon has come forward very strongly and has said that the officials of the railway can assess whether a line is going to be profitable and a self-liquidating venture and that if they find that to be so they can come here as prudent men and say, "Give us the money for this job and we will do it." But if there are going to be lines of the other type, those that are required to satisfy pressure groups, then I say that surely such people are the people who should be putting their signatures on the line as guarantors that in the future it will be a profitable operation. If we ever again embark on a system of building lines not on the basis of sound economic policy, we are going to remove the chance that in the future this may be one of the best paying railway operations that you will find.
One of the things that we in my area, and I suppose those in the greater metropolitan area of Toronto, are hoping for is that some of the new developments in railway operation we read about may become more beneficial in solving these problems of commuter service. I was most interested to read that the type of traffic control which has now been designed will make possible a great deal more use of the present roadbed or the present rails of the company. I am not going to read the evidence but I notice at page 157 Mr. Gordon at least went as far as to say that this new type of traffic control would make possible a greater use of the trackage. He was not going so far as to say that the stations in the present metropolitan areas were large enough to take care of the additional volume; but if all of these new automatic systems came in it might be possible that the position might change.
At the present time I think the answer is that there is no room or there is no track space available for the operation of commuter services on a large scale. With the new system of control it may be that we shall reach the position where there is room for that type of service, provided the actual depots themselves could be enlarged to take care of the additional volume of traffic. This consideration may be more important when we keep in mind the fact that he has indicated as well that the future for a considerable amount of passenger traffic may be not too bright. From the standpoint of the actual economic operation of the company, I do not think that he probably is going to complain too much about that because I think it is well known that the freight operations generally are the operations of the company which keep the over-all financial picture in the black. But when we have a combination
Canadian National Railways of those two factors, namely the new type of automatic controls enabling greater use of trackage in metropolitan areas and perhaps a falling off of the general line of passenger traffic that we have seen, it may be that in the larger metropolitan areas we may look for some relief for the commuter travelling public.
One other thing which it is most difficult for us to understand, I think, is that we have this continuation of financing of the national air line by means of a general omnibus resolution dealing with the national railway. It seems to me that some consideration should be given at an early date to seeing that the national air line is separated entirely in its financial responsibility from the railway company. We have heard that there are certain benefits in this type of operation; that there are certain departments where there can be a cutting down of personnel and where there may be a renting out of certain services, secretarial, legal and things like that. But it seems to me that we may be getting into the position in the over-all direction of the company where there could be a conflict of interest between the best course to be taken on behalf of the railway from the financing standpoint and the best course to be taken for the air line company. As a matter of fact, although I have not the figures before me, I believe that while the financing required now for Trans-Canada Air Lines is on a large scale, it will increase in the future because of the greater utilization of jet aircraft, bringing with it much greater expenditures. I believe that the financing of T.C.A. is going to be on a large enough scale that there will be no particular advantage or cost saving in continuing to have it included in this type of legislation.
I might say that perhaps this is a time when we might think of other methods of financing T.C.A. in any case. I notice that according to its statement they have about $20 million of debenture debt, $20 million of long-term loan from the national railway- these figures may not be exact-and about $6 million or $7 million of equity stock held by the railway company. It seems to me that there certainly might be an opportunity here for the people to see this company made into a large public corporation, but not on the basis of its being a national institution. If the people of Canada were given the opportunity perhaps to buy stock in the air line on the basis of a unit including a debenture and common stock, I do not think there would be the least bit of trouble in seeing that the whole capital requirements of T.C.A. were taken care of on a separate basis, with the people of Canada becoming equity shareholders on the basis of a common stock issue

Canadian National Railways along with the purchase of a debenture issue; maybe it might be five shares of common stock for every $100 bond that would be acquired. I think there would be great interest among the people of this country. I think there would be just as much interest as or more than that which my friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce had in the purchase of units of Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited.

I might say to the minister that if we had been given that first $150 million, almost anybody could go out and get the rest of it. But I believe there is here an opportunity to complete the financial set-up of this company. I think it is one that might be dealt with in a manner a little bit similar to the methods used in Alberta in connection with their gas distribution company, in which the public were given an opportunity to invest on a shareholder basis. Perhaps if the government wished to retain some control over this enterprise they could ensure, as they did out there, that a number of members of the board of directors should be of the government itself. As I say, I think it would create a renewed interest in the company and it would remove it from all the problems that may arise in dealing with it regularly in the House of Commons.
If there is any worry in connection with this particular problem from the standpoint of outsiders being in control of the company, I do not think we need to worry because, as I recall it, the Aeronautics Act provides that no more than 40 per cent of a company engaged in air transport in Canada may be owned by anyone of foreign nationality. Hence there would be here an opportunity of spreading the ownership on a businesslike basis and of making this company operate as does any other company in this business. These are things that I think should be said. We shall have more to say along these lines when the bill is presented to the house.

Will the Postmaster General explain to the committee the practice followed by the post office with regard to c.o.d. mail? Within the last day or two I have had a very bitter complaint from a constituent to the effect that a postman came to his home with a c.o.d. letter on which the sum of $1 was required. His wife paid the $1. It was a large brown envelope and when it was opened it was found to contain a copy of one of the Canadian magazines. I will not give the name of the magazine, although I shall be glad to show the minister the letter. By this time his wife had paid the $1 and it is apparently taken as constituting a subscription to this particular magazine. That seems to be a high-handed way to get new subscriptions, and I do not believe the post office should allow itself to be used for a purpose of that kind. The woman had no idea what was in the envelope, but the post office collected the $1 from her and now the family find themselves subscribing to a magazine they do not want. I do not think it is right for the post office to be used in that way.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, before you proceed with clause 1 of this bill I believe from looking at the evidence that there was considerable delay in connection with the proceedings in relation to this bill. I wonder if the sponsor could give the reasons for this delay or make any comments he might care to offer with respect to this bill.

Mr. Chairman, the printed evidence of the senate committee shows that the petition was first heard on January 16, 1957, at which time the hearing before the 82715-201
Private Bills-Divorce
senate committee was unopposed. The committee recommended that the divorce be granted and its report was adopted by the senate. The bill was given first reading on January 24. I agree with my hon. friend that there was considerable delay from the time it was agreed on the evidence that the divorce should be granted on January 16 to the time the bill reached the house.
After the evidence had been heard I was informed by those responsible for these bills in the other place that a letter was received from the respondent on January 25 in which she stated that she objected to the accusations contained in the petition but lacked money to defend herself. Steps were then taken which halted the progress of the bill and it was referred back to the committee. On January 31 the respondent was advised by registered letter that she would be given until February 15 to file a notice of objection and to make application for funds for the conduct of her defence.
No reply was received to the letter of January 31. The respondent was again advised by registered letter on February 18 that she would be given a further extension until February 25 to file her notice of objection. On February 27 the respondent acknowledged the letter of February 18 stating she wished to contest the matter and requesting funds for her defence.
On February 27 an order was made by the chairman of the said committee requiring the petitioner to pay the respondent $100. The Ottawa agent for the petitioner, the solicitors for the petitioner and the respondent were so advised and proof of the payment of the money to the respondent personally on March 9 was filed with the committees branch of the other place.
On March 14 the respondent was advised by telegram that the case would proceed if she did not file formal notice of opposition by March 18. As of March 19, the day after the time would have expired for her to file her notice of objection, no acknowledgment of the telegram or further indication of intention to oppose the petition was received by the committee branch of the other place.
I might summarize the situation by saying that this was a case that went before the Senate committee dealing with divorce and the bill was passed without any notice of objection having been filed. After it had been passed the respondent requested that she be given further time in which to file a notice of objection. As a matter of fact she was given several extensions of time. An order was put through under which the petitioner was to pay the respondent the sum of $100 and this was done.

Private Bills-Divorce
The committee branch was advised that she never did file a notice of objection before the Senate committee and the Senate naturally proceeded to refer the bill to the House of Commons.
I might say from my own investigation it has been revealed to those charged with the responsibility for procedure in this house in relation to the divorce committee that no notice of objection has been filed to date and therefore this bill has been allowed to proceed in the normal course.

Mr. Chairman, this is one of the contested cases which required a good deal of time before the senate committee. I find that the petitioner and his wife are Roman Catholics. In the course of the examination the petitioner's counsel made some enquiries about the wedding dowry. Apparently the husband was supposed to give his wife $100 a month plus $25 on the $5,000 promised to her in the wedding contract. His Honour Senator Roebuck asked the following question:
Are you still doing so?
His Honour was referring to the payment of $25 a month. The answer was as follows:
I am paying more than that because when the action was rendered by the judge my lawyer was in prison.
It was not brought out in evidence whether the lawyer referred to was the lawyer who was appearing for him who was in prison at the time. It is unfortunate that this matter was not followed up but it was left at that point. The following questions were asked of Mr. Petel:
Q. You did not defend yourself?
A. No, I didn't defend myself.
Q. Why not?
A. My lawyer told me not to defend myself in this case and to continue to try and watch her to have evidence and then proceed with something else.
Q. How much are you paying now?
A. Right now, sir, I am paying $132 a month.
Then there was some questioning about the petitioner leaving home for three months, after they had been married for three years. He was then asked:
Q. After those three months is is not true that you went back to the place where your wife was living to ask her to come back to start living together?
A. It is not exactly that way. I went on Christmas day to pay a visit to my son and I had a gift for him. When I came in that house she jumped at me crying, and then took me to her room and made me all kinds of promises that she would do well and she was willing to come back with me. I asked her to give me a little time to consider, maybe 15 days or three weeks; after we talked, we decided to go back together. I did not know any adultery had been committed at that time; I thought it was normal for me to do that.
Q. At the time you had no suspicion of adultery on your wife's part?
A. No I did not. That was three years after my marriage.
Then there is some cross-examination here:
Q. With your permission, Mr. Chairman; Was the purpose for you to get a divorce to save the allowance you are paying to your wife?
Petitioner's counsel then says:
Do not answer that at the present time.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The question itself is rather objectionable. What do you mean by it? Did you not close your cross-examination?

Then counsel for the corespondent says: I asked permission.
And then a little later on:
Q. Is it true that the purpose of your divorce is to save the obligations you have to your wife and child?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Yes, that is a little different from the way I was understanding it. Is the purpose of your divorce to save the expense that you are now under in making remittance to your wife and child.
And the petitioner's counsel withdrew his objection and the questions asked continue: Q. Go ahead witness.
A. My answer to that, sir, is that that is the reason for asking my divorce-that is one of the reasons.
Q. That is one of the reasons?
A. Yes.
And then there is a great deal more of examination and cross-examination and I wish to draw the attention of the committee to the fact that a 16-year old boy was called to the committee and he gave evidence to try to clear his mother's name:
Q. Tell me your full name.
And he gave it.
Q. What is your age?

Q. Where do you live?
And he gave his address.
Q. What is your occupation?
A. Office boy.
And the chairman then said:
I suppose you know the significance of an oath, do you witness?
And the little lad said yes.
Q. During the time your mother and father were living together was there something wrong between them?
A. Things were not getting along too nicely.
Q. Why?
A. They had many wrangles at home.
Q. About what?
A. About almost everything under the sun.
Q. Was there any discussion about the conduct of your mother?
A. No.
Q. Has your father in front of you made some reproach to his wife regarding her conduct?
A. No.
And again:
Q. Did you ever meet Mr. Parent at your home?
He is the corespondent.
A. Yes.
And then the young lad gave evidence to contradict the charges brought against his mother. In discussing the other cases we have taken the position that it is not our responsibility to present facts and figures to establish that these individuals appearing before the Senate and the Commons committee to get a divorce are perfect individuals, but it would appear to me that since this is a contested case and since relief 82715-201i
Private Bills-Divorce
is being given to a man of something over $5,000, this seems to be an important factor in this particular divorce and this committee and the house should not approve the divorce.
Clause 1 agreed to.

On clause 1, 1 have noted the hon. member who has just spoken mentioned this particular bill and I might say that I think it should be on the record that there is no objection registered with the committee branch of this house.
I wonder if the hon. member would speak a little louder.
I may say that there is no objection registered with the committee branch of this house that it should be opposed before the committee of this house.

I wonder if I may ask the sponsor of this bill if it is generally known that the respondents engaged in these cases have the privilege of presenting their grievances to the House of Commons committee which the hon. member chairs.

I would presume that if the respondent in this case was represented by counsel before the committee of the upper house that we should not assume the responsibility of counsel and, if she did not know, her counsel should have known. At any rate, there was no objection registered with the house, as I have pointed out, and therefore I recommend its passing by this committee.

Mr. Speaker, I must confess that I have not read all the evidence in connection with this case. The report which deals with it appears to be the longest report I have ever seen since I came to parliament many years ago. The last page is numbered 143.
I am sure hon. members may be excused if they have not been able to read carefully the whole of this evidence, especially since it is getting rather late in the session. However, there are one or two matters which I would like to draw to the attention of the house. As hon. members might expect, this is a contested case and it seems fairly clear to me that this is a case where there is a "frame-up". I do not have the dictionary definition of what constitutes a frame-up, but it would appear to me that this woman who is trying to prevent a divorce being granted was looking after a store and generally supplying the wherewithal to keep herself and her son while her husband was looking after himself.
There was a good deal of contradiction in connection with the evidence, as might have been expected. It is stated on page 103 that the husband wanted a divorce very badly. But the wife apparently was not agreeable to a divorce being granted. I find that the hon. senators who dealt with this matter followed the case very closely and appeared to have a good deal of sympathy with the wife. One hon. senator, for example, told the witness that he was going to ask her a question because he thought she needed "a little bit of help".
Q. You went out with this strange man and then you felt yourself in a compromising position?
A. That is right.
Private Bills-Divorce
What page is that one?

Page 111. Then on page 114 there are some questions and answers in connection with drinking. Apparently this strange man came into the store on a number of occasions. He was driving a valuable car and made a date to take the lady in question to a place where drinks were served. It appears they had a couple of martinis. I am not sure just what they are, but that appears in the record here somewhere. After having these martinis the strange man suggested that he had a bottle of rye in his car, and eventually they did make their way to a motel and apparently they had a drink of this rye in the motel. Almost at that point the husband's spies came down on them.
According to the information the respondent gives she had not been in the habit of going out to these places, but she had lived quite a lonely life for a number of years, keeping her little store open from 6.30 in the morning to eleven o'clock at night. I submit, that hon. members of this house should really not be expected to be familiar with the 143 pages of evidence presented in connection with a domestic problem of this sort and be able to reach a decision as to whether or not an act of parliament should be passed to grant the husband relief.
I might say just a few words in reply-
