speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The last time I spoke to this bill I said that Mr. Cartier had been before the Senate and the House of Commons two years ago and that this time the case was not re-heard in the other place. That statement is incorrect. A new hearing was conducted in the other place. What I should have said was that in the new hearing no reference was made to the fact that Mr. Cartier had been here two years ago.

Mr. Speaker, I moved the adjournment of the debate the last time this matter was before the house. To oblige members interested in this
Private Bills-Divorce
case we propose to have it go by on division but before it does I should like to say a few things. I should like to remind the house that in the Journals of the house for Friday, July 15, 1955 there is the following:
Mr. Hosking, from the standing committee on miscellaneous private bills, presented the tenth report of the said committee, which is as follows:
Pursuant to the order of the house of July 5, 1S55, your committee has reconsidered Bill No. 492 (letter S-16 of the Senate), intituled: "An act for the relief of Georges-Etienne Cartier", and has agreed to report the preamble thereof not proven on the grounds that they are not satisfied that adultery on the part of the respondent has been proven.
Some hon. members will recall that the appropriate committee of this house heard the evidence. I happen to have a copy of the evidence which was available at that time. I find that counsel for the petitioner were a well known Ottawa barrister, Mr. A. H. Lieff and Mr. Nat. W. Jacobs, barrister-at-law, of Montreal. I find that the detectives were Mr. Paquette, Mr. Brault, and Mr. Pichette of the Reliable or Fidelity detective agency. These detectives were in the news at that particular time for having fabricated evidence, but as apparently it was not illegal to fabricate evidence at that time with a view to granting this divorce, these men won their appeal and they were quite within their rights in coming before our committee to give evidence in this particular case.
I find that the petitioner has changed counsel. The counsel in this particular case is Mr. Hume, barrister, of Montreal. Apparently Mr. Lieff is still interested in this case. At this point I should like to register my objection to having representations made to me as a free member of parliament by counsel who have been or are interested in particular divorce cases before parliament. I think the members of this house should be free to discuss these cases and to draw their own conclusions without being influenced by people outside the house who had or still have some interest in connection with these particular cases. I find that this matter was before parliament two years ago. I took a little bit of the time of the house to review again the record of the detectives who gave evidence. In summing up, the learned judge who heard the particular case said this:
In my opinion, therefore, however contemptible the conduct of the appellants may be considered, they have not been proved guilty of the offence charged, and effect must be given to the legal position taken by their counsel. The point which has been raised in the instant case, apparently for the first time, would appear now to be academic, because the legislation is entirely changed in the new Criminal Code, . . .
At that time I quoted from the evidence which was placed before the Senate committee. I am reading from page 5595 of

Private Bills-Divorce
Hansard of 1955. I am referring to the evidence given by the two children, first of all that of Jean-Pierre, 13 years of age. That is two years ago. He would now be 15. I say this:
I find the following in the proceedings of the committee:
Then I read from the proceedings as follows:
Q. What would happen to you if you did not tell the truth?
A. I would commit perjury.
Q. What would happen to you if you did commit perjury?
A. I would go to prison.
Q. What would happen to your soul?
A. I would lose my soul.
Q. What is your name?
A. Jean-Pierre Cartier.
Q. What is your age?
A. Thirteen.
Q. Where do you live?
And he gives the address.
Q. What is your occupation?
A. Student.
Q. Who lives in the house with you, Jean-Pierre?
A. Myself, Suzanne, Mr. Bernier and my mother.
Q. And you said "Louis"?

No, he did not.
Then the interpreter said, "I did not hear 'Louis'
Then one of the counsel said: "He counted the names on his fingers and he said 'Louis'
The interpreter: Yes, Louis.
Then there was a question about where all the people sleep.
A. I sleep with Louis in my bedroom, Suzanne sleeps with my mother, and Mr. Bernier sleeps on the chesterfield in the living room.
Q. Does Suzanne go to bed before you?
A. We go to bed approximately at the same time, but sometimes earlier because she is younger.
Q. Have you seen her in bed' before you go to bed at any time?
A. It has happened.
Q. Where was she sleeping?
A. In my mother's bed.
Q. That is all.
Then the petitioner's lawyer said: "No questions".
Then I refer to the evidence of Suzanne Cartier.
Q. What is your name?
A. Suzanne Cartier.
Q. What is your age?
A. Nine.
Q. Where do you live?
And she gives the address.
Q. What is your occupation?
A. Student.
Q. Where do you sleep?
And that answer was given.
Then the petitioner's lawyer said "No questions".
Then the petitioner was recalled, and there is the following passage:
Q. How much do you make per month?
A. $250 or $260.
Q. And you are paying your wife $100 a month?

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
Q. Do you have anything else other than your salary?
A. No; I sometimes work overtime.
I should like to draw to the attention of the committee the fact that the detectives who have been retained in this particular

case have also been reprimanded in connection with the evidence they supplied. My colleague, the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) had occasion to discuss in the house the evidence of the detectives who came here in connection with this particular case. I understand that the chairman of the standing committee on miscellaneous private bills now has from the respondent a request to be heard. I think it is only right that hon. members should have a chance to hear whether there have been some developments in the last two years and that they should have a chance to examine these two detectives who gave the evidence on which the divorce is being recommended.

I should like to say a couple of words on this bill. Dealing with the first part of the statement made by the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson) may I say that I am quite sure he in his own mind, with his directly responsible reasoning, could not be changed or altered by any discussion of counsel on the facts.
As to the second part of it I am pleased that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) corrected his statement appearing in Hansard of April 2 at page 2983. But in order that there may be no mistake in the minds of the members of the committee, I might say that a perusal of the 1957 printed evidence discloses no reference to the 1955 evidence having been taken into consideration by the Senate committee on the hearing of the petition. It appears that the 1957 hearing was based on the alleged offence stated to have been committed after the former petition of 1955 had been disposed of and that the suspected co-respondent and the address at which the alleged offence was stated to have been committed were both the same as in the earlier petition. The witnesses appearing in 1957 were different from those appearing in 1955, except of course for the petitioner herself.
I have not seen any notice of objection that has been filed opposing this bill; it went through the Senate committee unopposed.
That is the situation at present. Unless something takes place after the reference of the bill by this house to the standing committee on miscellaneous private bills, I presume that there will be no objection on behalf of the respondent in this matter.

speechtext:
Tomorrow, Mr. Speaker, we shall start with the estimates of the Post Office Department. I understand the Postmaster General will not be able to be here after one o'clock so that after that we shall turn to the following bills: the second reading of the Canadian National Railways financing bill; the Prairie Grain Producers Interim Financing Act; the Windsor harbour commissioners; the north Pacific seal resolution; the eastern rocky mountain bill; the Senate amendments with respect to the Exchequer Court Act; and the Territorial Lands Act and the Currency, Mint and Exchange Fund Act. If they are completed then other items of legislation will be taken up in whatever manner might be indicated at that time.
May I also say that we have been asked on several occasions how much of this the government feels ought to be passed before prorogation and I should like to express my views on that so that hon. members may consider what I have to say. There is no reason why all the items on the order paper cannot be disposed of in the time we have left.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: How much time have we left?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
We have the time left between now and prorogation; but I should point out that still on the order paper after what I have listed there will be the hospitalization bill, the farm marketing legislation and the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, the three of which ought certainly to be put through, in our view, together with other legislation. I should add to that the Income Tax Act which has not yet been disposed of. Then it would be

desirable to clear up everything that is on the order paper, including an amendment to the Judges Act, notice of which, I think, has been given in Votes and Proceedings. May I also say that there are two or three tax conventions which have been signed in the last few days and which are available and while I realize they are not urgent in the sense that they must go through before the end of this session I think there are matters which are routine now and might very well be passed.
It seems to me that between now and prorogation we should dispose of the order paper and the estimates of the Post Office Department and interim supply in order that when we come back in the fall there will not be anything left over that could be disposed of now. I would suggest therefore that consideration be given to this and if it is the desire of hon. gentlemen opposite to have a supply motion which would be available to them to move a want of confidence motion on we would have to dispose of these matters before that could be done; or at any rate before we call it we would want to be reasonably certain we could dispose of the business I have mentioned.
This can take two forms, as I understand it. Under the rules as they are now a supply motion would have to be called on Monday and conclude on Tuesday night. I do not think there is any possibility that the house could devote two days to a supply motion. On the other hand we could supply a motion which by consent would be limited to one day, or alternately it could be agreed that perhaps the motion for interim supply when it comes could be subject to amendment, although it is not under the rules and Your Honour would stay in the chair while that motion was being discussed for some period of time, part of a day perhaps, but at any rate not exceeding a day.
I have placed the alternatives as I see them before the house. I think perhaps these alternatives might be considered so that even if we are not able to call a supply motion on Monday because of the uncertainty of getting the legislation through we might find it possible to meet the wishes of hon. gentlemen at a later time during next week.
